newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel revises GDP forecast down to 2.5 pct.
newsitem.headline: Israel revises GDP forecast down to 2.5 pct.

text.p: Israel's Treasury on Monday revised down its growth forecast for this year to 2.5 percent from earlier 4.1 percent, saying tight monetary policies and smaller tourism revenues were among the reasons.

The Treasury said per capita gross domestic product would edge up only 0.2 percent to 53,000 shekels ($14,900) while business sector GDP would expand 2.5 percent, down from a earlier projection of 4.5 percent.

"There are a number of factors that explain the slowdown," the Treasury said its forecast. "Some are the result of policy measures; the others result from natural economic processes or from external events."

It said these factors included that natural business cycle, declining immigration, restrictive fiscal and monetary policy and a deteriorating security situation, which caused a drop in incoming tourism.
The Treasury's revised forecast puts it closer to private sector estimates. The Bank of Israel on June 29 said it expected GDP to grow 2.5 to 3.0 percent.

In 1996, Israel's aggregate GDP grew 4.4 percent, its slowest rate in seven years, while per capita GDP expanded 1.7 percent. The Israeli economy expanded at a 6.1 percent annualised pace in 1990-1995.

In the meantime immigration is expected to fall to 60,000 this year from 71,000 in 1996 and an average of 114,000 annually in 1990-955. The immigrants had contributed to the economy's expansion by requiring housing, buying consumer durables and expanding the labour force.

About the only good news in a list of downward revisions is the deficit in Israel's current account, which the Treasury said would fall to $3.6 billion this year from a record $5.3 billion in 1996. The deficit as a percentage of GDP is also expected to decline to 3.6 percent from 5.6 percent in 1996 and an earlier Treasury 1997 projection of 4.7 percent.
One reason for the decline is a projected drop in Israel's civilian trade deficit to $9.9 billion this year from $11.4 billion in 1996.

Merchandise and service exports, the Treasury said, would grow 6.7 percent this year, an increase from 1996's 4.9 percent but down on levels seen earlier in the decade. Growth in civilian imports by comparison are expected to slow to just 1.8 percent, it added.

The Treasury said growth in private consumption is expected to fall to 2.3 percent this year from 5.5 percent in 1996 so that per capital private consumption would show no growth at all. Growth in domestic public consumption is also expected to slow to 1.9 percent from 3.5 percent in 1996.
Investment in fixed assets will shrink by 2.4 percent from 1996's level, the Treasury said, led by a 2.8 percent decline in investment in machinery and equipment.
The decline in investment marks a turnaround from several years of sharp growth. In 1990-95, investment grew an annual pace of 15.2 percent and rose 8.4 percent in 1996.
The Treasury said unemployment was now expected to swell to 7.7 percent this year, after a steady decline from a 1992 peak. ($ = 3.552 Israeli Shekels)
